claims.claim: The federal government is funded through twelve annual appropriations bills that Congress rarely enacts on time
claims.sourceSpan: the House and Senate Appropriations Committees have been organized in 12 subcommittees, with each subcommittee responsible for developing and managing the consideration of one regular appropriations act

claims.claim: All twelve regular appropriations bills have been enacted before the start of the fiscal year four times since FY1977, most recently for FY1997
claims.sourceSpan: Since FY1977, there have been four times when all regular appropriations bills have been enacted before the start of the fiscal year, most recently for FY1997.

claims.claim: One appropriations bill per Appropriations subcommittee, twelve in all

claims.claim: CRS: spending controlled through the appropriations process is known as discretionary spending

claims.claim: CRS: discretionary spending generally consists of funding for the operations of most federal agencies and most of the programs, projects, and activities each carries out

claims.claim: Subcommittee development of the bills typically begins shortly after the President submits an annual budget request
claims.sourceSpan: The subcommittees’ development of regular appropriations bills typically begins shortly after the President submits an annual budget request to Congress

claims.claim: The President is required to submit the budget request by the first Monday in February each calendar year under 31 U.S.C. 1105, although submission may sometimes be delayed
claims.sourceSpan: The President is required to submit the budget request for the upcoming fiscal year by the first Monday in February each calendar year (31 U.S.C. §1105), although the actual submission of the budget may sometimes be delayed.

claims.claim: Agencies submit detailed budget justifications to the Appropriations Committees laying out spending plans and how they used the prior year's appropriations
claims.sourceSpan: individual agencies and departments also submit detailed budget justifications to the Appropriations Committees

claims.claim: Subcommittees hold hearings with agency officials and collect input from Members who do not serve on Appropriations
claims.sourceSpan: they typically hold hearings to solicit the testimony of agency officials and question them about the agency’s budget request

claims.claim: Regular appropriations bills are often marked up by the subcommittees beginning in the spring
claims.sourceSpan: Regular appropriations bills are often marked up by the subcommittees beginning in the spring.

claims.claim: The subcommittee chair usually provides a draft bill known as the chair's mark
claims.sourceSpan: the subcommittee’s chairperson usually provides a draft bill (known as the chair’s mark)

claims.claim: The subcommittee votes on whether to forward the amended draft to the full committee, which marks it up again and votes to report it
claims.sourceSpan: the subcommittee votes on whether to forward the amended draft bill to the full committee.

claims.claim: Because House rules allow the Appropriations Committee to report an original bill, an appropriations bill is not formally introduced or numbered until the House Appropriations Committee reports it
claims.sourceSpan: Because House rules allow the Appropriations Committee to report an original bill, an appropriations bill is not formally introduced and assigned a bill number until the House Appropriations Committee reports it.

claims.claim: Committee report text is not in the legislative text, so it does not establish a statutory requirement or obligation the agency must follow
claims.sourceSpan: Because the text of these reports is not included in the legislative text, it does not establish a statutory requirement or obligation that the agency must follow.

claims.claim: Agencies tend to heed report language since it indicates congressional intent, and report language has sometimes been incorporated into statutory text by reference
claims.sourceSpan: In some instances, however, report language has been incorporated into the statutory text of appropriations acts by reference and become a part of the law.

claims.claim: The Congressional Budget Act provides for adoption of a concurrent resolution on the budget
claims.sourceSpan: The Congressional Budget Act (CBA) provides for the adoption of a concurrent resolution on the budget.

claims.claim: A concurrent resolution is not a law: the President cannot sign or veto it, it has no statutory effect, and no money can be raised or spent pursuant to it
claims.sourceSpan: Because a concurrent resolution is not a law, the President cannot sign or veto it, and it does not have statutory effect, so no money can be raised or spent pursuant to it.

claims.claim: The report accompanying the budget resolution allocates total budget authority among the committees with spending jurisdiction — the Section 302(a) allocations
claims.sourceSpan: an allocation of total budget authority among all committees with spending jurisdiction (commonly referred to as Section 302(a) allocations after the applicable section of the CBA)

claims.claim: An allocation under Section 302(a) effectively sets an enforceable ceiling on total appropriations
claims.sourceSpan: An allocation as required under Section 302(a) of the CBA, however, effectively sets an enforceable ceiling on total appropriations.

claims.claim: The Appropriations Committees subdivide the 302(a) amount among their subcommittees, effectively giving each subcommittee its own ceiling
claims.sourceSpan: The CBA further requires the Appropriations Committees separately subdivide the 302(a) amount among their subcommittees, effectively providing each subcommittee with its own ceiling.

claims.claim: Those subdivisions are the 302(b) suballocations, and they become effective and enforceable once the committees have reported them
claims.sourceSpan: These subdivisions are referred to as the 302(b) suballocations.

claims.claim: The House may consider regular appropriations bills after May 15 even if no budget resolution has been adopted and no 302(a) or 302(b) allocations made
claims.sourceSpan: The CBA provides that the House may consider regular appropriations bills after May 15 even if a budget resolution has not been adopted or 302(a) allocations or 302(b) suballocations made.

claims.claim: Without a budget resolution there may not be an enforceable upper limit on the overall level of appropriations
claims.sourceSpan: Without a budget resolution, there may not be an enforceable upper limit on the overall level of appropriations.

claims.claim: When agreement comes late or not at all the chambers use deeming resolutions, deemed to serve in place of an agreement between the two chambers for setting enforceable budget levels
claims.sourceSpan: These alternatives are typically referred to as “deeming resolutions,” because they are deemed to serve in place of an agreement between the two chambers on an annual budget resolution for the purposes of establishing enforceable budget levels

claims.claim: Since the 111th Congress the House has considered regular appropriations measures exclusively under the terms of special rules
claims.sourceSpan: Since the 111th Congress, it has considered regular appropriations measures exclusively under the terms of special rules

claims.claim: Special rules are House resolutions developed and reported by the Committee on Rules
claims.sourceSpan: These special rules are House resolutions that are developed and reported by the Committee on Rules.

claims.claim: Since the 115th Congress the House has exclusively used structured special rules for initial floor consideration of regular appropriations measures
claims.sourceSpan: Since the 115th Congress, the House has exclusively used structured special rules

claims.claim: Where several bills are combined, each separate regular appropriations bill is designated as a separate division and the special rules provide that each division is amended separately in sequential order
claims.sourceSpan: separate regular appropriations bill included is designated as a separate division of the bill. The special rules then provide that each division is to be amended separately in sequential order.

claims.claim: Once amending is complete the House votes on engrossment and third reading, a Member who opposed the measure may move to recommit, and the House then votes on final passage
claims.sourceSpan: Once the amendment process is completed, the House votes on the measure’s engrossment and third reading. At this point, a Member who opposed the measure may make a motion to recommit

claims.claim: The Senate lacks a procedural mechanism like the House Rules Committee and special rules for tailoring consideration of regular appropriations measures
claims.sourceSpan: The Senate lacks a procedural mechanism like the House Rules Committee and special rules that can be used to tailor its consideration of regular appropriations measures.

claims.claim: Appropriations measures enjoy no special privilege for consideration in the Senate, so a motion to proceed to them would be debatable in most circumstances
claims.sourceSpan: Because appropriations measures enjoy no special privilege for consideration in the Senate, a motion to proceed to their consideration would be debatable in most circumstances.

claims.claim: That subjects both the motion to proceed and the measure to the possibility of extended debate, commonly known as a filibuster
claims.sourceSpan: would be subject to the possibility of extended debate (commonly known as a filibuster)

claims.claim: The Senate can avoid extended debate through unanimous consent or overcome it by invoking cloture by supermajority vote
claims.sourceSpan: The Senate can avoid this possibility through the use of unanimous consent or overcome it by invoking cloture by supermajority vote.

claims.claim: Senate Rule XXII provides for cloture to be invoked by a vote of three-fifths of all Senators (60 votes if there is no more than one vacancy)
claims.sourceSpan: Senate Rule XXII provides for cloture to be invoked by a vote of three-fifths of all Senators (60 votes if there is no more than one vacancy).

claims.claim: Senate Rule XVI establishes general restrictions on amendments to appropriations bills, including prohibitions against amendments proposing general legislation or not germane to the bill's subject matter
claims.sourceSpan: Senate Rule XVI establishes general restrictions on amendments to appropriations bills, including prohibitions against amendments that propose general legislation or are not germane to the subject matter contained in the bill.

claims.claim: The Constitution requires that the House and Senate pass the same measure without any differences in the legislative text
claims.sourceSpan: the Constitution requires that the House and Senate pass the same measure without any differences in the legislative text

claims.claim: The simplest method is one chamber taking up a measure passed by the other and passing it without amendment; otherwise a conference committee or an exchange of amendments is used
claims.sourceSpan: The simplest method to achieve this result is for one chamber to take up a measure passed by the other chamber and pass it without amendment.

claims.claim: Regardless of the approach, the House bill has been the legislative vehicle ultimately enacted
claims.sourceSpan: Regardless of the approach, the House bill has been the legislative vehicle ultimately enacted.

claims.claim: When regular appropriations are not enacted in time Congress may use one or more continuing appropriations acts to provide interim funding
claims.sourceSpan: Congress may use one or more continuing appropriations acts (often referred to as a “continuing resolution” or a CR

claims.claim: A CR is usually comprised of three main components
claims.sourceSpan: The form of a CR differs from other appropriations acts and is usually comprised of three main components:

claims.claim: The first component is temporary appropriations continuing funding for the activities funded by the prior year's regular appropriations acts
claims.sourceSpan: temporary appropriations to continue funding for the activities funded by the prior year’s regular appropriations acts

claims.claim: The second is provisions limiting the agencies' use of that budget authority during the duration of the CR
claims.sourceSpan: provisions limiting the agencies’ use of that budget authority during the duration of the CR

claims.claim: The third is anomalies — additional provisions giving extra funding, exceptions to the CR's terms, or other legislative changes for specific programs or activities
claims.sourceSpan: additional provisions (commonly referred to as “anomalies”) that provide either additional funding, exceptions to the terms and conditions of the CR, or other legislative changes for specific programs or activities.

claims.claim: CRS: Congress has often taken procedural action to combine some or all of the regular appropriations bills into a single measure
claims.sourceSpan: Congress has often taken procedural action at some point in the appropriations process to combine some or all of the regular appropriations bills into a single measure.

claims.claim: A measure carrying several regular bills is referred to as an omnibus or consolidated appropriations measure
claims.sourceSpan: These measures are commonly referred to as “omnibus” or “consolidated” appropriations measures.

claims.claim: Consolidated appropriations legislation containing only some of the regular appropriations bills may also be referred to as a minibus
claims.sourceSpan: Consolidated appropriations legislation containing only some of the regular appropriations bills may also be referred to as a

claims.claim: Supplemental appropriations acts provide budget authority in addition to amounts provided by regular or continuing appropriations measures
claims.sourceSpan: Supplemental appropriations acts provide budget authority in addition to any amounts provided by regular or continuing appropriations measures.

claims.claim: Supplementals are usually developed in response to urgent and unanticipated needs, such as natural disasters and urgent military operations
claims.sourceSpan: These measures are usually developed in response to urgent and unanticipated needs, such as natural disasters and urgent military operations.

claims.claim: Appropriations legislation also provides funding for certain programs controlled by laws other than appropriations acts, known as appropriated entitlements or appropriated mandatories
claims.sourceSpan: Appropriations legislation also provides funding for certain programs controlled by laws other than appropriations acts, known as “appropriated entitlements” or “appropriated mandatories.”

claims.claim: GAO: the major types of appropriation act are regular, supplemental, deficiency and continuing
claims.sourceSpan: Major types of appropriation acts are regular, supplemental, deficiency, and continuing.

claims.claim: GAO: regular appropriation acts are all appropriation acts that are not supplemental, deficiency or continuing
claims.sourceSpan: Regular appropriation acts are all appropriation acts that are not supplemental, deficiency, or continuing.

claims.claim: REMOVED (the sweep's worst finding, independently re-confirmed): "At some point — sometimes during a government shutdown, sometimes just before one — Congress packages the remaining unresolved bills into a single omnibus spending bill and passes it as a year-end legislative vehicle." The FY2026 cycle resolved across FOUR public laws (119-37, 119-74, 119-75, 119-86), not one omnibus, and CRS IN12324 treats omnibus and minibus as co-equal outcomes. Replaced with the IN12324 wording and the actual four-law FY2026 record. This also removes the contradiction with the site's own audited omnibus-vs-minibus explainer.

REMOVED: "In practice, this has happened exactly once in the last thirty years", and the same claim in the title and meta description. Neither stored CRS source states a thirty-year framing; R47106 footnote 23 says four times since FY1977, most recently FY1997. Replaced with the sourced figure.

REMOVED: "roughly $1.7 trillion per year in recent budgets" for discretionary spending. No stored source carries it, and cbo.gov bot-walls scripted fetches, so it could not be sourced. Replaced with CRS R48731's qualitative definition of discretionary spending.

REMOVED: "the roughly 30% of federal spending that Congress appropriates annually. The other 70% is mandatory spending". Unsourced, and the framing is wrong in a way the stored source corrects: appropriations legislation also funds "appropriated entitlements" or "appropriated mandatories", so the two categories are not a clean partition of the budget.

REMOVED: "Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and other entitlement programs that flow automatically under permanent law and don't require annual appropriations" and "Mandatory spending cannot be cut by failing to pass appropriations bills". Uncited; the same uncited claim appears in government-shutdown.html and is not repaired here (different article, different batch).

REMOVED: "Social Security offices process checks, Medicare pays claims, and Medicaid continues during a shutdown because those programs operate under permanent funding authority." No stored source supports any of the three operational claims.

REMOVED: the twelve bullets' agency-to-subcommittee mapping (e.g. "DOJ, FBI, NASA, NOAA, Census Bureau"). R47106 footnote 5 defers agency placement to CRS R40858, which is not stored. Replaced with the departments each FY2026 act's own titles name, taken from the four enacted texts.

REMOVED: Defense described as "the largest bill by dollar amount" and Labor-HHS as "typically the most contentious non-defense bill". Neither is in any stored source; the second is a characterisation no source makes.
REMOVED: "Congress writes its own spending bills and routinely departs from the President's numbers." No stored source characterises the relationship this way.

REMOVED: "partisan disagreements over spending levels, abortion riders, environmental regulations, gun policy, immigration enforcement, and dozens of other policy issues make it nearly impossible to pass all twelve bills through a divided Congress before the deadline." An unsourced causal claim naming specific policy areas.

REMOVED: "A 2,000-page spending bill negotiated in a few days and passed by both chambers in hours leaves little time for members to read what they're voting on", "Policy riders ... slip into omnibus bills that would never pass as standalone legislation", and "Accountability is low and speed is high." Unsourced characterisations, one of them a page count no source supports.

REMOVED from Key Sources and the JSON-LD citation list: the House and Senate Appropriations Committee homepages and the CBO discretionary-spending topic page. None sourced any statement that survives. Replaced with CRS R47106, R48731, IN12324 and the GAO glossary, which do.

RECORDED, not a defect: two of the twelve carry a CRS subcommittee name that differs SUBSTANTIVELY from the enacted FY2026 act name - "State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs" was enacted as the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026, and the Transportation-HUD subcommittee name carries an extra "and". Four more (Defense, Homeland Security, Interior, Labor-HHS-Education) differ only by the routine "Department(s) of" prefix the act titles add, which is why the article states the difference for the first two and not the rest. The previous version silently picked one name and never showed the divergence at all.

claims.claim: REMOVED (round 1, hostile Sonnet source pass): three narrowings this audit introduced. (a) CRS hedges the committee timeline with "typically" in three places and the draft had dropped all three, turning usual practice into unqualified fact - restored. (b) An anomaly was described as only "exceptions to the CR’s funding rate or terms", when CRS gives three forms: additional funding, exceptions to terms and conditions, or other legislative changes - all three restored. (c) The May 15 condition was written as conjunctive ("no budget resolution AND no allocations"), narrowing the source’s disjunctive "has not been adopted OR 302(a) allocations OR 302(b) suballocations made" - corrected. Also corrected: the ledger note claiming only two subcommittee names diverge from their enacted act titles.
The deeming-resolution trigger is specific: when Congress has reached final agreement on a budget resolution AFTER APRIL 15, or has not reached agreement at all
claims.sourceSpan: When Congress has reached final agreement on a budget resolution after April 15 or has not reached agreement at all, the House and Senate, often acting separately, have used legislative procedures to deal with enforcement issues on an ad hoc basis.

claims.claim: REMOVED (round 2, hostile Sonnet source pass): "When agreement comes late or not at all" softened CRS’s specific trigger for deeming resolutions. Restored to the source’s own condition - final agreement on a budget resolution after April 15, or no agreement at all. Also improved: the ledger anchor for the four-public-law aggregate claim, which had cited one of the twelve section 101 entries rather than the enumeration itself.

notes: First-refresh audit of a May 2026 pre-lane explainer, Phase B session 5 of the article audit sweep, run immediately after appropriations-act-2026 and against the same stored source set. The sweep's worst finding — "Congress packages the remaining unresolved bills into a single omnibus spending bill", which contradicted the site's own audited omnibus-vs-minibus explainer — is REMOVED and replaced with the actual four-public-law FY2026 record. Twelve further claim families were removed rather than softened (see the removed.* rows), including every uncited quantitative claim in the article: the $1.7 trillion discretionary figure, the 30/70 discretionary-mandatory split, the "exactly once in thirty years" framing, and the twelve bullets' agency mapping, which R47106 footnote 5 defers to a CRS report that is not stored. The twelve-bill list is now built from primary sources only: CRS's subcommittee names, H.R. 9770 section 101's map of which law and division each FY2026 act landed in, and the department titles each enacted act itself carries. CONVERGENCE: three rounds. Round 1 = two hostile Sonnet passes (source-only; cross-page/editorial/structural), BOTH SIGN OFF with zero blocking findings but six real advisories, of which three were narrowings this audit had introduced (CRS hedges "typically" dropped in three places; the anomaly definition cut from three forms to one; the May 15 condition turned from disjunctive to conjunctive) - all restored. Round 3 = a targeted pass on a frozen file over the seven edited passages: SIGN OFF, 7 of 7 PASS with source quoted. Independently re-derived by script in the main thread: all 12 law-and-division pairs against H.R. 9770 sec 101, all 12 CRS subcommittee names, all 42 department title names matched to the correct enacting act (ruling out the right-title-wrong-act trap), and the nine-division/five-annual count from two separate primary sources.
